title: Open Your Mouth Wide
sum: Psalm 81 is Psalm 80 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It begins as a festival song, with drums, lyres and the ram's horn at the new moon and the full moon, and then turns into a sermon. A voice the singer did not know (81:5) speaks for God: I freed you from slavery, I answered you in the storm, I am the LORD your God. Open your mouth, and I will fill it. But my people would not listen.

The psalm holds out what Israel could have had, enemies humbled and the best of the wheat and honey from the rock, and grieves that it did not happen. The festival is probably the autumn Feast of Booths, when Israel remembered the wilderness and, every seventh year, heard the law read aloud (Deuteronomy 31:10–13). Jewish tradition hears the new year, Rosh Hashanah, in its shofar.
readings: Read as a festival liturgy

The psalm fits a worship service: a call to praise (81:1–5), then a priest or prophet speaks God's word (81:6–16), reminding the people of the exodus and the first commandment. Each year's festival renewed the covenant, and the warning was part of the celebration.
Read as God's lament

God speaks like a disappointed parent: "Oh, if my people were listening to me" (81:13). The psalm shows a God who wants to give and is refused, and who still keeps the offer open. The last line is still an offer: "I would fill you with honey from the rock."

views.H: The title names Asaph, David's music leader, and "the gittith". Reading the title as history, the psalm belongs to the Asaph singers of the Temple. Its "Joseph" (81:5) and its stress on the exodus and the wilderness suggest the northern tribes, and some link the Asaph group to Bethel or Shechem before their songs came south.
views.C: Form critics see a prophetic liturgy for the autumn festival. Mowinckel took it as evidence of a covenant renewal festival, where the Ten Commandments were recited (81:9–10 echoes Exodus 20:2–3). Its links with Deuteronomy and Hosea point to the eighth or seventh century BC, though some date it after the exile.
views.L: The Latin of 81:16, cibavit eos ex adipe frumenti ("he fed them with the fat of the wheat"), is the entrance chant for the feast of Corpus Christi, so the psalm became a Eucharistic song in the Western church.
views.J: In the Second Temple the Levites sang Psalm 81 on Thursdays (Mishnah Tamid 7:4). Its verses on the shofar at the new moon (81:3–4) are recited on Rosh Hashanah, and the Talmud uses them to show that the new year is God's day of judgment (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 8a–b).
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 81:16 the bread of life and in "honey from the rock" the gift of Christ, the rock that followed Israel (1 Corinthians 10:4). Augustine read "open your mouth wide" as an invitation to desire God himself.

echoes: Exodus 20:2–3; Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 20:13; Deuteronomy 32:13–14; Deuteronomy 31:10–13; Leviticus 23:24; Numbers 10:10; Jeremiah 7:23–24; Acts 7:42; Romans 1:24; 1 Corinthians 10:4

settings.what: A festival call to worship, then an oracle from God
settings.by: a Temple singer or prophet (the title: Asaph), speaking God's words in 81:6–16
settings.to: Israel gathered at the autumn festival; in 81:6–16 God addresses the people directly
settings.when: at the new moon and full moon of the festival month, probably the Feast of Booths (the title gives no occasion; the rabbis say Rosh Hashanah)
settings.why: to turn a feast into a covenant moment: to remind the worshipers who freed them, to repeat the first commandment, and to warn that blessing depends on listening
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile heard it as an explanation of their history ("So I left them to the stubbornness of their hearts") and as an offer still open. In the Temple it became the Thursday psalm.
views: Part of a regular ceremony in which the law was recited and the covenant renewed (Mowinckel, Kraus).
The new year festival with its shofar blasts, as Jewish tradition reads 81:3.
Composed among the northern tribes ("Joseph") and later brought to Jerusalem (Nasuti).

deep.h: The witnesses for Psalms 81–89, and which were checked
deep.b:
The Hebrew. The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008). The Masada Psalms scroll (MasPs-a), copied before AD 73, preserves about 81:2–85:6 and is reported to agree closely with it, mostly differing in spelling (Talmon). At Qumran, 4QPs-e holds bits of Psalms 76–89, and 4Q236 is a short, rearranged copy of the oracle in 89:20–31 (see the note on 89:20). These scroll readings are taken from the published reports (Talmon; Flint; the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible); the scrolls and DJD editions were not seen.

Checked directly for this part: the Old Greek in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus as Swete prints them; Jerome's Gallican Psalter and his Psalter from the Hebrew (the latter also in Lefèvre d'Étaples' Quincuplex Psalterium of 1513 at 89:2 and 89:17); the Targum of Psalms; Rashi; Ibn Ezra; and Midrash Tehillim. Reported, not checked: the Syriac and the readings of other Hebrew manuscripts, given as listed in BHS.

title: You Are Gods
sum: Psalm 82 is Psalm 81 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In eight verses it shows a scene in heaven: God rises in the assembly of El and puts the gods on trial. Their crime is injustice. They have taken the side of the wicked and left the weak, the orphan and the poor without defense, and so the foundations of the earth are shaking. God's verdict follows: "I said, 'You are gods'... Yet you will die as humans die." The singer ends by asking God himself to rule the earth.

Few short texts have been read in so many ways. Most modern scholars see the divine council of the ancient Near East, the gods of the nations judged and condemned. Jewish tradition and many Christian interpreters saw human judges, or Israel at Sinai. Jesus quotes 82:6 in John 10:34 to answer a charge of blasphemy. The psalm also gave Eastern Christianity a key text for theosis, and Latter-day Saints a text for exaltation.
readings: Read as the trial of the gods

The "gods" are heavenly beings to whom God gave the nations (Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the Greek and Dead Sea Scrolls). They have ruled unjustly and will die like humans. The psalm announces the end of every power but God's, and hopes for the day when he will "take all the nations as your own" (82:8).
Read as a word to judges

The "gods" are human judges, called elohim because they judge in God's place (Exodus 21:6; Exodus 22:8–9). God warns them that their office does not exempt them from death or from his judgment. This was the reading of the Targum, Rashi and Calvin.

views.H: The title names Asaph. As history, it would be a Temple singer's prophetic word against corrupt judges or against the gods of the nations. Nothing in the psalm ties it to a single event.
views.C: Scholars compare the council of El at Ugarit, where the high god El sits among "the sons of El". Many date the psalm to the monarchy or the exile and read it as a turning point: the God of Israel declares the other gods unfit and mortal, a step toward monotheism (Mark Smith). Others find a polemic against the idea that other gods existed at all.
views.L: In the Byzantine rite of Holy Saturday, 82:8, "Arise, O God, judge the earth", is sung with the psalm's verses as the clergy change to white vestments and scatter bay leaves: Christ has risen to judge the powers.
views.J: The Levites sang Psalm 82 on Tuesdays (Mishnah Tamid 7:4). The Mishnah says that where ten sit and study, or three judge, God is among them, citing 82:1 (Mishnah Avot 3:6). The Targum and Rashi made the "gods" judges; the Talmud read 82:6–7 of Israel at Sinai, made like angels and losing it with the golden calf (Bavli Avodah Zarah 5a).
views.X: Jesus answers the charge that he made himself God by citing 82:6 (John 10:34–36). The fathers took "gods" as the redeemed, made sharers in God's nature (2 Peter 1:4); Athanasius wrote that the Son became human so that we might become divine. Reformed and Lutheran readers stressed rulers' accountability: Luther's 1530 commentary on Psalm 82 is a manual for princes.

deep.b:
1. Divine beings. The setting is "the assembly of El" (82:1), the same council of "holy ones" and "sons of the gods" that praises God in 89:5–7. The gods are called "sons of the Most High" (82:6), and their punishment is that they will die "as humans die" (82:7), which only means something if they were not human. Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in the Greek and in a Dead Sea Scroll says the Most High divided the nations "by the number of the sons of God", keeping Israel for himself. Psalm 82 then shows those rulers failing and God taking back the nations (82:8). This reading is held by most critical scholars and by some evangelicals (Michael Heiser).

2. Human judges. The Law sometimes calls judges elohim (Exodus 21:6; Exodus 22:8–9), and the charges are a judge's sins: crooked rulings, favoritism, neglect of the poor (82:2–4; compare Deuteronomy 1:17). The Targum renders "the assembly of the righteous" and "true judges"; Rashi, Calvin and many Protestant commentators follow. The difficulty is 82:7: why say judges will die "as humans die"?

3. Israel at Sinai. The Talmud says that when Israel received the law, the angel of death had no power over them; God said, "You are gods". After the golden calf he said, "Yet you will die as humans die" (Bavli Avodah Zarah 5a). This reading connects the title "gods" with the giving of God's word.

deep.h: "The Scripture cannot be undone": Psalm 82 in John 10
deep.b:
When Jesus said "I and the Father are one", his hearers took up stones, saying he made himself God. He answered: "Your own law has it written, doesn't it, 'I said, You are gods'? So, if he called those people gods, the people the word of God came to, and the Scripture cannot be undone, then the one the Father made holy and sent into the world, do you say to him, 'You blaspheme,' because I said, 'I am God's Son'?" (John 10:34–36).

The argument is from the lesser to the greater. If Scripture can call others "gods", it is no blasphemy for the one God sent to call himself God's Son. "The people the word of God came to" fits the Sinai reading best (Jerome Neyrey): Israel received the word and was called "gods". It may also fit the judges (God's word came to them in the law), or even the council. Christians differ on what Jesus implies: some hear a modest claim (the title is not blasphemy), others a strong one (he is God's Son in a way the "gods" never were). Calling the Psalms "your law" shows that "law" could mean the whole of Scripture.

deep.h: Psalm 82 at Qumran: Melchizedek as judge
deep.b: A Dead Sea Scroll, 11QMelchizedek (11Q13, first century BC), quotes 82:1 and applies it to Melchizedek, a heavenly figure who will judge Belial and his spirits on the day of atonement at the end of days: "God stands in the council of God" refers to him. It also cites 82:2 against Belial's followers. The scroll shows that some Jews before Jesus read the psalm of heavenly beings, and that one of them, not God himself, might carry out God's judgment. The scroll is cited here from the published translations (Vermes; Abegg, Flint and Ulrich).

echoes: John 10:34–36; Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Psalm 89:5–7; Psalm 58:1–2; Exodus 21:6; Exodus 22:8–9; Deuteronomy 1:17; Isaiah 24:21–23; 1 Kings 22:19–23; Job 1:6; Daniel 7:9–10; 2 Peter 1:4

settings.what: God's trial of the gods, with a closing prayer
settings.by: a prophetic singer (the title: Asaph) who reports what he sees in heaven and quotes God's verdict (82:2–7)
settings.to: the "gods" of the council (82:2–7), then God (82:8); overheard by Israel at worship
settings.when: no occasion is named; the Temple sang it each Tuesday
settings.why: to assure the weak that injustice on earth is judged in heaven, to warn every power that it answers to God, and to pray for God's direct rule over the nations
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, ruled by foreign empires and their gods, heard that those powers were already condemned and that God would take the nations as his own.
views: The heavenly patrons of the nations are judged (Mullen, Smith, Tate).
A warning to human judges (Targum, Rashi, Calvin).
God's word to Israel, made immortal and then mortal again (Talmud).

traditions.q: "You are gods": can human beings share God's nature?
views: Yes, by grace: salvation is theosis, being made partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4) without becoming God by nature. Athanasius: the Son "became human that we might become god"; Vladimir Lossky.

The Word became flesh to make us "partakers of the divine nature"; the Catechism quotes Athanasius and Aquinas on deification (Catechism 460). The "gods" of Psalm 82 are usually read of judges or the saints.
Psalm 82 speaks of rulers, called gods because they hold God's office; they must protect the poor and will answer to God (Luther, 1530). Union with Christ is stressed, but not as a change of nature.
Magistrates are called gods because God's authority is committed to them (Calvin, Institutes 4.20.4); the psalm is not about human deification.

Faithful men and women may become gods through exaltation; the Doctrine and Covenants says of the righteous, "they are gods, even the sons of God" (Doctrine and Covenants 76:58; compare Doctrine and Covenants 132:20), and Psalm 82:6 and John 10:34 are cited as support.
The "gods" were Israel's human judges, called gods as God's representatives; Jesus cited the verse to show his claim to be God's Son was not blasphemy.

title: Do Not Keep Silent
sum: Psalm 83 is Psalm 82 in the Greek and Latin numbering, and it is the last psalm of Asaph. It is a community lament against a coalition of ten nations, from Edom and Moab to Philistia, Tyre and Assyria, who plot to wipe Israel's name from memory. The people ask God to break his silence and do to them what he did to Midian and to Sisera in the days of the judges.

Its curses are fierce: make them like tumbleweed, chase them with your storm. Yet the purpose it names is that they will "search for your name, LORD" (83:16) and learn that the LORD alone is Most High (83:18). No known war brought all ten together, so the list may be a poetic sum of Israel's neighbors and enemies.
readings: Read as a war prayer

A real threat lies behind it, perhaps in the Assyrian age, when Assyria (83:8) backed smaller states. The people remind God of his victories under Gideon and Deborah (Judges 4–8) and ask for the same.
Read as a picture of every enemy

Ten names, and the whole circle of neighbors, make a symbolic coalition: the world against God's people. Read this way, the psalm is a prayer whenever a people is threatened with destruction, and it ends hoping even enemies will know God.

views.H: The title is "A song. A psalm of Asaph." 2 Chronicles 20 tells of Moab, Ammon and Mount Seir attacking Jehoshaphat, with a Levite of Asaph's family, Jahaziel, prophesying victory (2 Chronicles 20:14). Some link the psalm to that war, though the lists differ.
views.C: Most scholars see a national lament. Because Assyria is a helper, not the leader, many date it before Assyria's great conquests, in the ninth or eighth century; others take it as a later stylized list. A Maccabean date was once proposed and is now rarely held. The ten nations may be meant to echo the ten nations of Genesis 15:19–21.
views.L: The Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves Psalm 83 out of its four-week cycle, with 58 and 109, because of its curses (General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 131). It is prayed in full in the monastic Psalter and in the Orthodox Psalter, where it is Kathisma 11.
views.J: Midrash Tehillim hears the plot as aimed at God himself: as long as Israel exists, he is called the God of Israel. The Targum names the Assyrian helper of 83:8 as Sennacherib, and Rashi says Assyria, which had once left Nimrod's evil counsel, now joined the wicked. Many Jews have prayed the psalm in times of threat.
views.X: Christian readers have prayed 83 against spiritual enemies, and have stressed 83:16 and 83:18: the goal of judgment is that God's name be known. Augustine read the shame of the enemies as a call to conversion.

echoes: Judges 4:1–24; Judges 7:1–25; Judges 8:4–21; 2 Chronicles 20:1–30; Genesis 19:36–38; 1 Chronicles 5:10; Isaiah 17:13; Exodus 15:11; Ezekiel 38–39

settings.what: A community lament against a coalition
settings.by: a Temple singer for the people (the title: Asaph)
settings.to: God, asked to speak and act
settings.when: a threat from a league of neighbors; no single war matches the list
settings.why: to bring the threat before God, to remind him of past victories, and to ask that the enemies be shamed until they seek his name
settings.readers: After the exile, Israelites surrounded by hostile neighbors (Edom, Ammon, Philistia and the rest appear again in Nehemiah's time) could pray it as their own.
views: Ninth or eighth century, while Assyria was still a backer of others (Kraus).
2 Chronicles 20, the Asaph Levite's victory oracle (some traditional readers).
Ten names standing for all Israel's enemies (Hossfeld and Zenger).

traditions.q: Psalm 83 asks God to destroy a league of nations. Should the church pray it?
views: The Roman Liturgy of the Hours leaves Psalm 83 out of its four-week cycle, with 58 and 109, because of its curses (General Instruction 131); it is kept in the monastic Psalter and in Scripture readings.
The whole Psalter is read each week; Psalm 83 (Greek 82) stands in the eleventh kathisma and is prayed in full, its enemies read as the passions and the demons.
The 1662 Book of Common Prayer reads every psalm in its monthly cycle, Psalm 83 included; some modern Anglican psalters mark harsh verses as optional.
Churches that sing only the psalms sing it whole, as God's word against God's enemies, leaving vengeance to God (compare Calvin on the psalm).

title: How Dearly Loved Your Dwellings
sum: Psalm 84 is Psalm 83 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It is a pilgrim's song of longing for the Temple. The singer envies the sparrows nesting by the altars and the Temple staff who live there; then he follows the pilgrims through a dry valley that turns to springs as they walk, "from strength to strength", to Zion.

Its best-known line weighs time with God against everything else: "One day in your courtyards is better than a thousand." A prayer for the king (84:8–9) suggests the monarchy, while the closing blessings spread to everyone who trusts God. With 85, 87 and 88 it belongs to the second group of Korah psalms, a counterpart to 42–49.
readings: Read as a pilgrimage song
It traces the journey: longing at home (84:1–4), the road (84:5–7), prayer on arrival (84:8–12). Pilgrims sang it on the way to the three festivals.
Read as a song of the soul

Christian and Jewish readers have heard it as the soul's longing for God, the Temple standing for God's presence. Brahms set its verses 1, 2 and 4 in A German Requiem for the dwelling of the dead with God.

views.H: The title gives the gittith and "the sons of Korah", the Levite singers and gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 9:19; 26:1). "I choose to stand at the threshold" (84:10) fits a family that kept the Temple doors.
views.C: Scholars classify it as a song of Zion and a pilgrimage psalm, probably for the autumn festival, when the first rains came (84:6). The prayer for "your anointed" (84:9) points to the monarchy; some read it of the high priest after the exile.
views.L: Sung at the dedication of churches in the Latin and Anglican traditions. Brahms's fourth movement in A German Requiem ("Wie lieblich sind deine Wohnungen") is its most famous musical setting.
views.J: 84:4, "Happy are the ones who live in your house", with 144:15, introduces Ashrei (Psalm 145) three times a day. 84:12 is said in the evening prayer and at Havdalah at the end of the Sabbath.
views.X: Augustine read the valley of weeping as this life and the pilgrims' strength as grace. Hebrews' picture of believers as pilgrims seeking a city (Hebrews 11:13–16; 13:14) lies close to it.

echoes: Psalm 42:1–4; Psalm 27:4; Psalm 122:1–2; Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16; 1 Chronicles 9:19; Joel 2:23; Hebrews 11:13–16; Hebrews 13:14; Revelation 21:3

settings.what: A pilgrim's song of longing for the Temple
settings.by: a pilgrim or a Levite singer (the title: the sons of Korah)
settings.to: the LORD of Armies, with a blessing on pilgrims and a prayer for the king
settings.when: on the way to Jerusalem for a festival, probably the autumn feast
settings.why: to voice the joy of coming to God's house and to make the long road part of the worship
settings.readers: After the exile, pilgrims from the scattered communities sang it on the way to the rebuilt Temple, and those who could not go prayed it as their longing.
views: Sung by pilgrims coming up for Booths (Kraus, Tate).
The prayer for the anointed shows a Temple service during the monarchy.

title: Loyal Love and Faithfulness Meet
sum: Psalm 85 is Psalm 84 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It looks back on a time when God forgave his people and "turned Jacob's fortunes back" (85:1), and then prays that he do it again, because his anger seems to last. A voice then listens for God's answer and hears peace.

Its closing picture is one of the most loved in the Psalter: loyal love and faithfulness meet, righteousness and peace kiss, faithfulness sprouts from the earth and righteousness looks down from heaven. Medieval Christians made the four virtues into four daughters of God, reconciled at the Incarnation, and the psalm became a song of Advent and Christmas.
readings: Read as a prayer after the exile

The people have come home (85:1–3), but life is hard and God still seems angry (85:4–7). The psalm fits the disappointment of the years after the return (Haggai 1:5–11) and promises that the land will give its crops (85:12).
Read as a promise of salvation
The oracle of 85:8–13 is open-ended: God's glory will live in the land, and righteousness will walk ahead of him. Christians hear the coming of Christ, "truth sprung from the earth" (Augustine).

views.H: The title names the sons of Korah. Read as history, 85:1–3 recalls a past restoration, perhaps the return from Babylon.
views.C: Scholars call it a community lament with a prophetic oracle, probably from soon after the return from exile (538 BC and after). Its language of turning (shuv) runs through the whole psalm.
views.L: The Western liturgy uses it in Advent: the versicle Ostende nobis, Domine, misericordiam tuam, from 85:7, is a classic of Advent, and Benedixisti, Domine, terram tuam (85:1) is sung in Advent. The Book of Common Prayer appoints it for Christmas Day morning.
views.J: A midrash tells that when God made humanity, Loyal Love and Righteousness argued for it, Truth and Peace against; God threw Truth to the ground, and "faithfulness sprouts out of the earth" (Genesis Rabbah 8:5).
views.X: Bernard of Clairvaux made 85:10 a drama of the four daughters of God, Mercy, Truth, Justice and Peace, reconciled when the Son became incarnate. Augustine read 85:11 of Christ born of Mary, truth from the earth.

echoes: Isaiah 32:15–18; Isaiah 45:8; Haggai 1:5–11; Haggai 2:9; Zechariah 8:12; Psalm 126:1–6; Psalm 89:14; Luke 2:14

settings.what: A community prayer for renewal, with God's answer
settings.by: a Levite singer for the people (the title: the sons of Korah); in 85:8–13 a prophetic voice reports God's answer
settings.when: after a restoration that has not brought the hoped-for blessing, probably after the return from exile
settings.why: to ask God to finish what he began, and to promise the people that his rescue is close
settings.readers: The returned exiles, living in a poor land under Persian rule, sang it as hope that God's glory would return to the Temple and the land.
views: After a drought or a defeat, with an earlier restoration in mind.

title: Make My Heart One
sum: Psalm 86 is Psalm 85 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It is the only psalm credited to David in Book III, a prayer of a poor man, hunted by violent people, who calls himself God's servant. Much of it is woven from other psalms and from God's self-description at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), quoted in 86:15.

Its center is a confession that no god is like the LORD, that all nations will come and bow to him (86:9), and a prayer for an undivided heart: "Make my heart one, so that it fears your name" (86:11).
readings: Read as an anthology prayer
Almost every line echoes another psalm. Scholars see a prayer composed from the language of worship, giving words to anyone in need.
Read as David's prayer
The title makes it David's, the servant king, praying when hunted; Jewish and Christian readers have heard his voice in it.

views.H: "A prayer of David", like the title of 17. It stands alone among the Korah psalms, perhaps added to link Book III with David.
views.C: Most scholars date it late, after the exile, because of its many borrowings (Exodus 34:6; Psalm 25; Psalm 54; Psalm 40) and its universal hope (86:9).
views.L: In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is the psalm of Night Prayer on Monday. Its first verse, "Bend your ear down, LORD", is a common opening for prayers.
views.J: 86:8, "Lord, among the gods not one is like you", is sung when the Torah scroll is taken out on the Sabbath, followed by 145:13 and 29:11.
views.X: Revelation's song of the Lamb echoes 86:9: all nations will come and worship (Revelation 15:4). Christian readers have heard in "your servant girl's son" (86:16) the voice of Christ, son of Mary, who called herself the Lord's servant (Luke 1:38).

echoes: Exodus 34:6–7; Psalm 25:4–5; Psalm 54:3; Psalm 40:17; Psalm 116:16; Revelation 15:4; Isaiah 2:2–4; Jeremiah 32:39

settings.by: a poor and faithful servant of God (the title: David)
settings.when: under attack by "arrogant men" (86:14); no event is named
settings.why: to plead for rescue on the basis of God's character as he revealed it at Sinai, and to vow undivided worship
settings.readers: After the exile, individual Israelites in danger used it as a ready-made prayer, joined to the hope that every nation would one day worship the LORD.
views: Composed after the exile from older phrases (Hossfeld and Zenger).
A king's prayer, "your servant" being the king (some scholars).

title: Born in Zion
sum: Psalm 87 is Psalm 86 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In seven short, puzzling verses it pictures Zion as the birthplace of the nations. God enrolls Egypt ("Rahab"), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush among those who know him, and writes beside each name, "This one was born there."

Israel's oldest enemies are counted as citizens of God's city. The Greek made it "Mother Zion", and John Newton's hymn "Glorious things of thee are spoken" (1779) began from 87:3. Its Hebrew is so compressed that some scholars think the verses have been displaced.
readings: Read as a vision of the nations
Foreign peoples are registered as natives of Zion: they will come to know the LORD and belong to his city (Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 19:23–25; Zechariah 8:20–23).
Read of the Jewish diaspora
The "ones born there" are Jews living in Egypt, Babylon and Cush, who still count Zion as home. Some scholars and some Jewish readers prefer this narrower reading.

views.H: The title names the sons of Korah. Its world (Egypt, Babylon, Tyre, Cush) fits the time of the monarchy and after.
views.C: A Zion song. Many date it after the exile, when Jews lived across the empires, and debate whether it means converts or diaspora Jews. The text may be disturbed: some move 87:5b after 87:1.
views.L: Sung at feasts of the church and of the Virgin Mary in the West, because of "Mother Zion". Newton's hymn, set to Haydn's tune, is sung widely in Protestant churches.
views.J: The Talmud reads "one after another was born in her" as both the one born there and the one who longs to see it (Bavli Ketubot 75a). The Targum makes the ones born there David and Solomon.
views.X: Paul calls the Jerusalem above "our mother" (Galatians 4:26), and Hebrews speaks of the city of the firstborn enrolled in heaven (Hebrews 12:22–23). Christian readers hear the church of all nations.

echoes: Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 19:23–25; Isaiah 60:1–14; Zechariah 8:20–23; Psalm 46:4; Psalm 48:1–3; Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22–23; Revelation 21:24–26

settings.what: A song of Zion, mother of nations
settings.by: a Levite singer (the title: the sons of Korah), quoting God in 87:4
settings.to: Zion, addressed as "city of God" (87:3), and the worshipers
settings.when: probably at a festival in Jerusalem; the date is debated
settings.why: to praise Zion as the city God loves and to declare that peoples far beyond Israel belong to it
settings.readers: After the exile, with Jews scattered from Egypt to Babylon and some foreigners joining the LORD (Isaiah 56:6–7), it gave both a place in Zion.
views: Foreign nations enrolled as citizens of Zion (most commentators).
Jews born abroad still counted as Zion's children (some scholars).

Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken

title: My Companions Are the Dark
sum: Psalm 88 is Psalm 87 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It is the darkest prayer in the Bible. A man who has been ill and near death since boyhood cries to God day and night. He feels already counted among the dead, laid in the pit, cut off from God's hand, shunned by friends, overwhelmed by God's anger like waves. He asks whether the dead can praise God, and nothing answers.

Unlike every other lament, it never turns to trust or thanks. It ends with the word "dark". Yet it opens by calling the LORD "God of my rescue" and is spoken to God from start to finish. Its place in Scripture has given permission to pray when there is no light at all.
readings: Read as the prayer of the sick

Lifelong illness, isolation (88:8), and the nearness of death fit a person with a chronic disease, perhaps a skin disease that forced him to live apart. It is a sick person's prayer, without the usual happy ending.
Read as the voice of Israel or of Christ
Rashi heard Israel in exile; Christians from the early church on heard Christ in his passion and in the tomb on Holy Saturday, counted among those who go down to the pit (88:4).

views.H: The title is double: a song of the sons of Korah and a maskil of Heman the Ezrahite, one of David's chief singers and one of the sages Solomon outdid (1 Kings 4:31). "On mahalath leannoth" may be a tune.
views.C: Scholars classify it as an individual lament with no turn to praise, unique in the Psalter. Its many names for the underworld show Israel's ideas of death before belief in resurrection was common. It is impossible to date.
views.L: In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is Friday's Night Prayer psalm, the day of the cross. Its verses are a Holy Saturday responsory, "Aestimatus sum". In the Orthodox Church it is one of the six psalms read at the start of Matins.
views.J: Rashi reads it as Israel in exile, "sick with love". Jewish readers have turned to it in grief and in the hiding of God's face, especially after the Holocaust.
views.X: Christian tradition hears Christ: abandoned by friends (Luke 23:49), laid in the grave, among the dead. The psalm's questions in 88:10–12 are answered at Easter. Pastors give it to the depressed and dying as a prayer that does not pretend.

deep.h: A psalm that does not resolve
deep.b: Laments usually move from complaint to trust. Psalm 22 ends with praise; Psalm 13 ends with a vow to sing. Psalm 88 has three cries (88:1, 88:9, 88:13), each followed by a fuller description of misery, and no turn. Its last words, "my companions are the dark", leave the speaker where he began. Some scholars think the reason is simply honesty: some suffering does not lift, and Israel kept a prayer for it. Others note that the psalm still speaks to God, calls him "God of my rescue", and keeps praying "every single day" (88:9): the act of prayer is itself the faith. In the Psalter it is followed at once by Psalm 89, which begins with God's loyal love, and Book IV opens with Moses' prayer to God as Israel's home in every generation (Psalm 90:1); the editors placed the darkness in a larger story without changing a word of it.

deep.h: Sheol in Psalm 88, and the later hope
deep.b: The psalm gives the fullest Old Testament picture of the world of the dead: Sheol, the pit, the grave, Abaddon, darkness, the land of forgetting, the shades (see the notes). The dead there are weak, forgotten, cut off from God's hand, and they cannot praise him (88:5, 88:10–12). This was not a denial of God's power over death (1 Samuel 2:6; Deuteronomy 32:39) but a statement that worship belongs to the living. Later Scripture answers the psalm's questions. Isaiah 26:19 says "your dead will live" and the shades will rise; Daniel 12:2 speaks of many who sleep in the dust awakening. Jewish tradition came to confess the resurrection of the dead in its daily prayer. Christians read the psalm through the death and resurrection of Jesus, who went where the psalmist feared to go. Traditions differ on what the dead experience before the resurrection; see the card below.

echoes: Psalm 6:5; Psalm 30:9; Psalm 115:17; Psalm 22:1; Psalm 31:11–12; Psalm 89:1; Job 10:20–22; Job 17:13–16; Jonah 2:2–6; Lamentations 3:1–9; Isaiah 38:18–19; Isaiah 26:19; Luke 23:49

settings.what: A lament from the edge of death
settings.by: a sufferer who has been ill since youth (the title: Heman the Ezrahite, of the sons of Korah)
settings.when: in long illness and isolation; some read prison or exile
settings.why: to keep speaking to God when there is no answer and no hope left, and to plead for rescue while the speaker can still praise
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile kept it as a prayer for the darkest times, of a person or of the people in exile, without softening it.
views: A chronically ill man, perhaps isolated by disease (Tate, Kraus).
A prisoner in a pit, like Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:6).

traditions.q: Psalm 88 says the dead cannot praise God. Are the dead aware, and may the living pray for them? (The text every view here argues over is 2 Maccabees 12:45, where Judas had atonement made for the dead "to free them from the sin"; 2 Maccabees is held as Scripture by the Catholic and Orthodox churches but not by Protestants or Jews, and its card, "Can sins be cleansed after death, as the Catholic teaching on purgatory holds?", sets out the views.)
views: The soul lives on after death and is judged; Christ went down to the realm of the dead to free the just who had gone before (Catechism 632–635). The church prays for the dead in purgatory (Catechism 958, 1030–1032).
Christ descended into Hades and broke its power, as Holy Saturday celebrates. The departed are alive in God, and the church prays for them in memorial services until the resurrection.
The dead in Christ rest in him until the resurrection; masses and prayers to release souls from purgatory are rejected (Smalcald Articles II.2).
At death the souls of the righteous go at once to God and those of the wicked to hell (Westminster Confession 32.1); prayer is not to be made for the dead (21.4).

Death is an unconscious sleep; the dead do not praise God because they know nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:5), and they wait for the resurrection (Fundamental Beliefs 26). Psalm 88 is read as a plain description of death.
Sheol is the common grave of mankind, a state of non-existence; the dead are unconscious until God raises them.

title: Where Are Your Loyal Loves?
sum: Psalm 89 is Psalm 88 in the Greek and Latin numbering, and it ends Book III. It is the Psalter's great poem on the covenant with David. It sings God's loyal love and faithfulness (89:1–18), retells the promise God made through Nathan (89:19–37, compare 2 Samuel 7), and then accuses God of breaking it: the king's crown is in the dirt, his walls broken, his throne thrown down (89:38–45).

The psalm ends with questions, "How long, LORD?" and "Where, Lord, are your first acts of loyal love?", and with a blessing that closes Book III. It is the boldest protest in the Psalms, because it holds God to his own oath. Jewish readers heard in its last verse the footsteps of the Messiah (89:51); the New Testament proclaims Jesus as David's son on his throne.
readings: Read as a lament for the fall of the monarchy

The hymn and the oracle set up the crisis: if God swore the dynasty would last "like the sun" (89:36), how can the king be overthrown? The psalm likely speaks after Jerusalem's fall to Babylon (587 BC). It does not give up the promise; it calls on God to keep it.
Read as a messianic psalm

Jewish and Christian readers both read the promise forward. The Targum and the rabbis waited for the Messiah whose coming the mockers deride (89:51); the New Testament calls Jesus the firstborn and faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), and David's descendant raised to his throne (Acts 2:30; Acts 13:22–23, 34).

views.H: The title names Ethan the Ezrahite, a sage of Solomon's time (1 Kings 4:31). Read as history, Ethan foresaw the fall of David's line, as Ibn Ezra held; the Talmud identifies him with Abraham.
views.C: Most scholars see three parts, perhaps of different ages: a hymn with old mythic language (89:1–18), an oracle that reworks 2 Samuel 7 (89:19–37), and a lament from the exile (89:38–51), with the doxology (89:52) closing Book III. Nahum Sarna called it a case of inner-biblical interpretation. Gerald Wilson argued that Books I–III end here with the failure of the monarchy, and Book IV answers with psalms proclaiming that the LORD is king.
views.L: In the Catholic lectionary 89 is the responsorial psalm of the Christmas Vigil and of the feast of St Joseph, David's descendant. The Book of Common Prayer appoints it for Christmas evening. Mozart set 89:1, "Misericordias Domini" (K. 222).
views.J: 89:52 begins a group of verses in the evening service outside Israel; 89:15 is said after the shofar on Rosh Hashanah; "olam chesed yibbaneh" (89:2) is a proverb and a song. Ibn Ezra records a Spanish sage who could not bear to read the psalm because of its accusations.
views.X: The New Testament draws on 89 for Jesus as David's son (Luke 1:32–33), the firstborn and faithful witness (Revelation 1:5), the one whose reproach Moses bore (Hebrews 11:26), and the fulfillment of "the sure mercies of David" (Acts 13:34). Christians read the lament as answered by the resurrection.

deep.b:
Psalm 89:19–37 retells Nathan's oracle (2 Samuel 7:8–17; 1 Chronicles 17:7–15). Set side by side in the site's Plain, the two texts share the core and differ in telling ways. A Qumran fragment, 4Q236, preserves the oracle alone (89:20–31) in a shorter, rearranged form, which some take as an early stage of the psalm (see the note on 89:20; reported, not seen).

  • A vision. "Nathan passed on to David all these words, the whole of this vision" (2 Samuel 7:17). Psalm: "Back then you spoke in a vision to your loyal ones" (89:19).
  • The servant chosen. 2 Samuel 7:8 recalls how God took David from the flock; the psalm: "I have found David my servant / and anointed him with my holy oil" (89:20).
  • Enemies. 2 Samuel 7:9–11: "I wiped out all your enemies ahead of you"; "Evil men will not go on crushing them as they did at first". Psalm 89:22–23: "no man of evil will beat him down. / His attackers I will smash before his eyes". The psalm's ben-'avlah, "man of evil", is nearly the same phrase as the Hebrew behind 2 Samuel 7:10's "evil men".
  • Father and son. 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me." Psalm 89:26–27 turns it into the king's prayer, "You are my Father", and adds what Nathan did not say: "I will make him firstborn, / most high over the kings of the earth."
  • Sea and rivers. Only the psalm sets the king's hand "on the sea, / his right hand on the rivers" (89:25), sharing the victory over chaos sung in 89:9–10.
  • The condition. 2 Samuel 7:14: "If he does wrong, I will correct him with a rod such as men use, with blows such as people give." Psalm 89:30–32 makes it plural and legal: "If his sons turn their backs on my law / and do not live by my rulings... I will call their rebellion to account with the rod, / and their guilt with blows." 1 Chronicles 17:13 leaves the condition out.
  • Love not withdrawn. 2 Samuel 7:15: "But my loyal love will not turn away from him the way I took it from Saul." Psalm 89:33: "Yet my loyal love I will not break off from him."
  • For all time. 2 Samuel 7:16: "Your throne will stand firm for all time." Psalm 89:29, 36–37 add the heavens, the sun and the moon as measures.
  • Covenant and oath. 2 Samuel 7 uses neither word. The psalm calls the promise a covenant (89:3, 28, 34, 39) and an oath sworn by God's holiness (89:3, 35, 49), as David's last words already did: "For he has set up a covenant with me that lasts forever" (2 Samuel 23:5).
  • No Temple. In 2 Samuel the promise turns on a play on "house": "He will build a house for my name" (2 Samuel 7:13), and God will build David's house. Psalm 89 never mentions the Temple; it says only that God will "build your throne" (89:4).

The effect is to make the promise as strong as possible. The psalm removes every loophole: the sons may be punished, but the covenant cannot be broken, and God has sworn it. That sets up the accusation of 89:38–45, which uses the same words in reverse: "You have disowned the covenant of your servant; / you have profaned his crown" (89:39), against "My covenant I will not profane" (89:34).

deep.h: Was the covenant broken? How Book III ends, and the answers
deep.b:
The psalm does not answer its own question. Several answers grew up around it.

Inside the Psalter. Gerald Wilson argued that the editors arranged Books I–III around David's line, from Psalm 2's coronation to Psalm 89's fallen crown. Book IV (90–106) opens with Moses (90:0) and with the psalms that proclaim that the LORD reigns (93:1; 97:1; 99:1): when the human king fails, God himself is king, as before there was a monarchy. Book V returns to David in hope (110; 132; 144).

In the prophets. Isaiah 55:3 offers "an everlasting covenant, the faithful acts of loyal love promised to David" (fresh rendering) to all who come and listen, using the psalm's words: the promise passes to the people. Jeremiah 33:20–21 says the covenant with David could be broken only if day and night could be.

In Judaism. The Targum and the rabbis read "your anointed" as the Messiah and the mockery as the long delay before he comes (89:51; Mishnah Sotah 9:15). The doxology (89:52) became a blessing said every evening. Ibn Ezra defended the psalm's boldness and read it as hope for the Messiah.

In the New Testament. Gabriel tells Mary that God will give her son "the throne of his father David" and that "of his kingdom there will be no end" (Luke 1:32–33, fresh rendering). Peter (Acts 2:30–36) and Paul (Acts 13:22–37) argue that God kept the oath by raising Jesus from the dead, "the sure mercies of David". Christians differ on whether that throne is now in heaven or still to come on earth; see the card below.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the two Ezrahites at the end of Book III
deep.b: 1 Kings 4:31 names Ethan and Heman, both Ezrahites, as the wise men Solomon surpassed. The only psalms credited to them stand side by side at the close of Book III: Heman's personal darkness (88) and Ethan's national darkness (89). Perhaps the editors chose the names of the wise whom Solomon outdid to voice the questions that royal wisdom could not answer, just before Book IV turns from David to Moses. This is Claude's suggestion, not an established view; the pairing of 88 and 89 is often noted, but the link to 1 Kings 4:31 as a reason for the placement is not.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:8–17; 1 Chronicles 17:7–15; 2 Samuel 23:5; Psalm 2:7; Psalm 132:11–12; Psalm 110:1–4; Isaiah 55:3; Jeremiah 33:20–26; Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30–36; Acts 13:22–23; Acts 13:34; Hebrews 11:26; Revelation 1:5; Revelation 3:14; Colossians 1:15

settings.what: A hymn to God's loyal love, and the promise to David retold
settings.by: a Temple singer (the title: Ethan the Ezrahite), quoting God's oath (89:3–4) and Nathan's vision (89:19–37)
settings.to: the LORD ("you" throughout), with the congregation listening
settings.when: perhaps in Temple worship celebrating the king; or composed as the setup for the lament that follows
settings.why: to praise the God who rules the heavens and the sea, and to lay out his promises to David in their strongest form
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, with no king on the throne, these verses were a promise held up to God and a ground of hope for an anointed one to come.
views: The hymn and oracle come from the monarchy, perhaps a royal festival (Clifford).
All composed after 587 BC as a single lament (Veijola).

settings.what: A lament over the rejected king, and the closing doxology of Book III
settings.by: the singer for the people, speaking also as "your servant" and "I" (89:47, 50)
settings.to: the LORD, accused and then called on to remember
settings.when: after a disaster to the Davidic king, most likely the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC or Jehoiachin's exile in 597 BC; 89:52 was added by the editors to close Book III
settings.why: to hold God to his oath, to ask how long the shame will last, and still to bless him
settings.readers: The community after the exile, ruled by Persia, prayed it as its own question about the promise to David, and closed Book III with "Amen and amen".
views: 587 BC, the end of the kingdom of Judah (most scholars).
The young king exiled in 597 BC (89:45, "his youth").
A yearly rite in which the king was humbled and restored (older Scandinavian scholarship); now rarely held.

traditions.q: Is the promised throne of David filled now, or still to come?
views: Jesus is the Son of David whose kingdom has begun; the church is the seed and beginning of that kingdom on earth (Luke 1:32–33; Lumen Gentium 5; Catechism 439, 669).

Christ took David's throne at his resurrection and ascension (Acts 2:30–36) and reigns now; the promises to David are fulfilled in Christ and his church, with their completion at his return (Anthony Hoekema).

David's throne is an earthly throne in Jerusalem. Christ now sits at the Father's right hand, and will sit on David's throne in the millennial kingdom, when the promises to Israel are literally kept (Walvoord; Pentecost). Progressive dispensationalists say the Davidic reign has begun in heaven and will be completed on earth (Blaising and Bock).
Jesus, the heir of David, began to rule as king in heaven in 1914; his kingdom will soon replace human governments.
